claims.text: The shell gives every command it starts three standard streams already connected: standard input, standard output and standard error.
claims.source_hint: POSIX.1 Base Definitions, 'Standard I/O Streams'; Bash Reference Manual, 'Redirections'

claims.text: When a command is run from an interactive shell with no redirection, standard output and standard error are both attached to the terminal, so ordinary results and failure messages appear together on screen.
claims.source_hint: Bash Reference Manual, 'Redirections' (default file descriptors 0, 1, 2 of a simple command)

claims.text: `|` between two commands connects the standard output of the left command to the standard input of the right command; no temporary file is involved.
claims.source_hint: Bash Reference Manual, 'Pipelines'; POSIX.1 Shell Command Language, 'Pipelines'

claims.text: The commands of a pipeline start at the same time and run concurrently; the right-hand command reads while the left-hand one is still writing. When matches are frequent, `grep ... | head -3` over a very large file answers long before the whole file is read.
claims.source_hint: Bash Reference Manual, 'Pipelines' (each command in a separate subshell, executed concurrently); POSIX.1 Shell Command Language, 'Pipelines'

claims.text: A program reading standard input does not have to be told where the lines come from: `grep`, `head` and `wc` read a file, a terminal and a pipe the same way.
claims.source_hint: POSIX.1 Base Definitions, 'Standard I/O Streams'; grep/head utility descriptions (operand omitted means standard input)

claims.text: `grep PATTERN FILE` writes the lines of FILE that contain PATTERN to standard output and drops the others.
claims.source_hint: POSIX.1 utility 'grep', description and stdout section; GNU Grep manual, 'Invoking grep'

claims.text: `cut -d' ' -f4-` cuts each input line at every single space and writes the fourth field through the last; on the log lines of the example repository this drops the date, the time and the word `ERROR`, leaving the message.
claims.source_hint: POSIX.1 utility 'cut', options -d and -f (range 'n-'); GNU coreutils manual, 'cut invocation'

claims.text: `uniq -c` collapses only lines that are adjacent and equal, and prefixes each written line with the number of occurrences; this is why `sort` has to run before it for a count over a whole file.
claims.source_hint: POSIX.1 utility 'uniq', option -c and 'repeated lines in the input shall not be detected if they are not adjacent'; GNU coreutils, 'uniq invocation'

claims.text: `sort -n` compares lines by the numeric value at the start of the line and `-r` reverses the order, so `sort -rn` puts the largest count first.
claims.source_hint: POSIX.1 utility 'sort', options -n and -r; GNU coreutils manual, 'sort invocation'

claims.text: `> file` sends standard output to that file and truncates it to zero length first; `>> file` sends standard output to the file and adds after what is already there.
claims.source_hint: Bash Reference Manual, 'Redirecting Output' and 'Appending Redirected Output'; POSIX.1 Shell Command Language, 'Redirection'

claims.text: `>` redirects standard output only, so a failure message written to standard error still reaches the terminal; `2> file` is the redirection that captures standard error, the `2` being the descriptor number standard error carries in both `2>` and `>&2`.
claims.source_hint: Bash Reference Manual, 'Redirections' (file descriptor 1 is the default for >; 2> names descriptor 2)

claims.text: `>&2` in `echo "..." >&2` makes that echo write to standard error instead of standard output; the `&` marks 2 as a descriptor number, whereas `>2` would write to a file named `2`.
claims.source_hint: Bash Reference Manual, 'Duplicating File Descriptors' (>&word)

claims.text: `grep -c` writes the number of matching lines, not the number of matches within them; in the captured output of `scripts/terminal/pipes.sh` at stage-0 a six-line file gives `3`.
claims.source_hint: POSIX.1 utility 'grep', option -c ('write only a count of selected lines'); outputs/stage-0/scripts/terminal/pipes.txt

claims.text: In the captured output of `scripts/terminal/pipes.sh` at stage-0, `ls /nowhere` writes `ls: cannot access '/nowhere': No such file or directory` to standard error, `2> errors.txt` puts it in that file, and `cat errors.txt` prints it back.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang outputs/stage-0/scripts/terminal/pipes.txt; POSIX.1 utility 'ls' (diagnostic messages on standard error)

claims.text: `wc -l` writes the number of lines of its input, and writes the file name beside the count when the file arrives as an operand; `wc -l < file` gives the file through standard input instead, so only the count appears. At stage-0 `lab/app.log` gives `37`.
claims.source_hint: POSIX.1 utility 'wc' (output format with and without a file operand); outputs/stage-0/scripts/terminal/find-errors-in-log.txt

claims.text: At stage-0, `lab/app.log` holds 37 lines, one per event, each written as date, time, a level word (`ERROR`, `WARN`, ...) and a message separated by single spaces; 6 lines contain `ERROR` and 5 contain `WARN`.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang lab/app.log at stage-0; outputs/stage-0/scripts/terminal/find-errors-in-log.txt

claims.text: `grep -n` prefixes each written line with its line number in the input file; at stage-0 the first three `ERROR` lines of `lab/app.log` are lines 6, 8 and 16, and `grep -n ERROR` without `| head -3` lists all six.
claims.source_hint: POSIX.1 utility 'grep', option -n; outputs/stage-0/scripts/terminal/find-errors-in-log.txt

claims.text: `head -3` writes the first three lines of its input and `tail -1` the last one.
claims.source_hint: POSIX.1 utilities 'head' and 'tail', option -n / obsolescent -number

claims.text: At stage-0 the counting chain over `lab/app.log` reports the payment timeout message 3 times, the failed notification email 2 times and the database deadlock once.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang outputs/stage-0/scripts/terminal/find-errors-in-log.txt

claims.text: grep, cut, sort, uniq, head, tail and wc are present in the Git Bash terminal and in the Linux lab box. At stage-0, `grep WARN lab/app.log | cut -d' ' -f4- | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` prints four lines: the slow payment gateway message with count 2, then three with count 1.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang lab/app.log at stage-0 (run the chain against it); outputs/stage-0/scripts/terminal/find-errors-in-log.txt for the ERROR equivalent

claims.text: `grep PATTERN missing.log` with no such file writes a diagnostic naming the file to standard error and creates nothing on standard output, so `> found.txt` leaves an empty file.
claims.source_hint: POSIX.1 utility 'grep', 'Standard Error' and exit status 2; Bash Reference Manual, 'Redirecting Output' (the file is created and truncated before the command runs)

claims.text: In the example repository at stage-0, line 5 of `scripts/terminal/find-errors-in-log.sh` (the second line of the quoted block) tests whether the run is already inside the lab box and, if not, starts the same file again in there, where the repository is at `/repo`.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang scripts/terminal/find-errors-in-log.sh line 5, scripts/lab-run.sh, docker-compose.yml service `lab`

In `scripts/terminal/pipes.sh` at stage-0, `cd /tmp` moves the run to a scratch folder and `printf 'a
b
a
c
a

' > letters.txt` writes a six-line file there (three `a`, two `b`, one `c`); `printf` adds no line ending of its own, you spell it `
`, where `echo` adds it.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang scripts/terminal/pipes.sh lines 7-8 at stage-0; POSIX.1 utilities 'printf' and 'echo'

claims.text: When a running system misbehaves and its log is reachable, searching that log with `grep` and `tail` is usually where you start, before opening the code or adding new tools.
claims.source_hint: no document expected; condition stated in the sentence (outline item 4 of the lesson entry in track.yaml)

claims.text: An assignment `name=value` gives a value a name in the shell, and `$name` inside double quotes is replaced by that value wherever it is written; inside single quotes it is not.
claims.source_hint: POSIX.1 Shell Command Language, 'Variable Assignment' and 'Parameter Expansion'; Bash Reference Manual, 'Shell Parameters'
